coherence.reasons: Both follow the same sound arc (bridge, labor is 13%, hours cut feeds shrink, sized actions, sequence) and both tie summary lines to slide titles. X's governing thought carries the actual outcome (about 2.3%, 3.0% only if nearly everything goes right), and every later layer agrees with it: the waterfall, the low/base/high cases, the comparison with the draft and the covenant slide. Y's hierarchy has internal tension. Its headline says six actions reach 3.1% and the first three lift operating income to $33M, clearing the covenant. The supporting slide then concedes only $1.5M of headroom and an uncounted $7.3M wage rise, which would erase the headline. The covenant claim also uses full run-rate value in the first year. Y's slide title says 3.1% 'on FY2025 sales' while the figure is computed on $1,412M after exits. X has one minor overlap (moving hours out of Q4 stores and also cutting Q4 hours in the high case), which is smaller than Y's gap between headline and caveat.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the 8% hours cut and the e-commerce freeze, keep delivery with the tested fee, prune loss-making promotions, redeploy hours against shrink, grow private label and exit six stores at lease end. That matches the key's preferred recommendation. Y's plan nominally adds up to the 3.0% target and makes a clear ask for a board vote on the three long-lease exits, which is defensible. But it gets there only by assuming no wage inflation, although the pack states a 4% rise in 2027 that Y itself sizes at $7.3M. It also assumes chain-wide shrink falls to the best quartile's 2.3% while hours are merely moved. X weighs the trade-offs more honestly. It builds the wage rise and delivery-rate rise into the base case, gives a low case if promotions only return to the FY2024 share, and shows what it takes to reach 3.04%. It concedes that the management draft looks safer for the covenant on paper, defers the $7.5M exits with a stated reason, and recommends lender talks as a fallback. X's base case falls short of the target, but it says so and shows the path, which is more defensible before a board and a lender than a 3.1% headline with no margin for known headwinds. Neither pushes the e-commerce redesign beyond the tested fee and renegotiation.

evidence.reasons: The core numbers are correct and nearly identical in both: the margin bridge (79% and 13%), the gross-margin decomposition, the $10.4M e-commerce drag, the rebuttal of the 6.1% claim, $6.6M for nine stores split $4.4M and $2.2M, and $10.5M on promotions. Y's fee-test build is more itemised and applies cannibalisation consistently to lost online sales ($153K), and its $9.04 loss per delivered order at the tested fee is a useful check. X is stronger elsewhere. It splits the e-commerce loss per order ($12.34 delivered against $1.64 click-and-collect, 91% from delivery). It notes the category team's comparison does not control for store location or ValuMart, where Y only says it 'counts sales, not profit'. Its central estimate of the shrink offset applies only the staff-sensitive 65% (net $8M), with the full-attribution $4.5M as a sensitivity; Y headlines the upper-bound $10M offset. X sizes the shrink gain from the quartile pattern (Q1 and Q2 to the Q3 rate, Q4 has slack), which is better grounded than Y's whole chain at 2.3%. Y's covenant inference, full-year run-rate of three actions giving $33M in FY2026, is invalid without ramp or baseline drift; X computes the 29% threshold and states the condition that the decline must stop. Y's 3.1% leaves out the wage rise the pack announces. X arguably overstates that rise by applying 4% to the whole labor bill, but it shows the case with the rise offset.

revision.reasons: Both revise the CFO/COO hypothesis as the key expects, on the same quantified grounds: wages rose 9.4%, hours per $1,000 fell 6%, labor is 0.3 pp or 13% of the decline, and low-labor stores have the highest shrink. Both reject the freeze because it preserves the e-commerce loss. X is somewhat more balanced in what it keeps from management's view. It treats wage pressure as real and continuing by carrying the 2027 rise into the forecast. It identifies where hours can safely come out (Q4 stores are only 0.1 pp better than Q3). It evaluates the draft on its own terms, including the FY2026 covenant where the draft looks safer and an FY2028 outcome of about 1.3%. Y revises correctly but more one-sidedly: it cancels the cut, uses the upper-bound shrink offset as its headline and sets aside the future wage rise that is the valid core of management's concern.

overall.reasons: The two documents share the diagnosis and most of the levers, with nearly identical and correct core calculations. They differ in how honestly the plan is tested against the target and the covenant. Y gives the CEO a cleaner story (3.1%, covenant cleared at $33M, vote on three exits), but it rests on no wage inflation despite a stated 2027 rise, full run-rate delivery in the covenant year and an ambitious shrink target. Its own footnotes show $1.5M of headroom against a $7.3M uncounted headwind. X tells the board the realistic base case is about 2.3% and gives low and high scenarios with the specific extra moves needed for 3.0%. It quantifies how much of wave 1 must land to hold the covenant, admits where the draft plan is safer, and prompts early lender talks. X also handles the category team's claim and the shrink offset more carefully. That is the more decision-useful and defensible document for a CEO facing a board and a lender, even though its base plan falls short of the target.
